title: Citroën 2CV4: how to judge badly damaged floors without dismissing the base too quickly
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: In the Doubs, the floors of this 2CV4 were already badly damaged, yet the car still kept its interest. Here is how to separate heavy corrosion from a base that can still be saved.
content:
On the first walk around the car in the Doubs, the problem was visible without taking anything apart: the floors were badly eaten. On a 2CV, that alone is sometimes enough to walk away. Yet here the car was complete, close enough to the workshop, not stripped and still coherent enough to justify a real inspection. The point is to read corrosion properly instead of confusing a large job with a hopeless shell.

Look wider than the hole in the floor

A perforated floor draws attention because it looks dramatic. It should not hide everything else: shell alignment, state of the mounting points, presence of the doors and panels, visible chassis condition and the car’s general stance. A 2CV can have very tired sheet metal and still keep a usable structure if the rest has not been stripped or bent beyond reason.

That is why our reading of this 2CV4 did not stop at the holes. The engine was still in place, the cabin was still there, the wings were present and the car had not been obviously pillaged. A base stays interesting when the whole car still makes sense, even if the underside already promises many hours of metal work.

What corrosion changes straight away

Badly damaged floors immediately change three things: budget, time and method. Budget rises because cutting, fitting, welding and protecting must be done properly. Time expands because dismantling has to go further. And method changes because there is no point in trying to restart the car before the underside has been opened up honestly.

That has to be accepted before the purchase. If the plan is a quick service, a few brakes and an easy restart, a 2CV with dead floors is the wrong car. If the aim is a complete and honest restoration base, that corrosion alone does not necessarily end the story.

Price, distance and completeness matter too

The final judgement never comes from one defect alone. In our case, the price was considered fair, the Doubs was not six hundred kilometres from the workshop and the car had not been stripped of its main parts. Those three facts matter. An imperfect but nearby and complete base can still be more rational than a shinier car that is dearer and much farther away.

That is often where a good decision is made on a small French classic. The goal is not to deny corrosion but to place it inside a full file: condition, distance, logistics, present parts and the real aim of the job. A dead floor is serious; it does not automatically cancel everything else.

The real diagnosis starts at the workshop

The flatbed return does not close the matter, it opens it. Once the car is back in Rioz, the underside has to be checked again, older repairs read properly and the reusable areas separated from the metal that must be replaced. That colder reading, under good light and with tools, turns a buying instinct into a useful diagnosis.

The full discovery of this base remains on the parent page Citroën 2CV4: a complete base found in the Doubs. For the buying angle, the companion draft on judging a non-running 2CV4 extends these checks.
